title: Dances created for songs: Charleston, Ballin' the Jack
summary: He argues that dance and music are linked, and discusses authorship of the Charleston and other songs.

story.theme_name: Playing for dancers: dance bands and the dances themselves
story.community_name: Dancing to the band: quadrilles, waltzes and dance sets

blocks.x: He was a dancer. And...you know, strange as it seems...as it may seem to you, to many people...lay people, persons...
wherever there was a style of music played or a song created, did you know they created a dance to go along with it?

For example, you take like the Charleston. James P. wrote that song, "The Charleston." James P. should have become the richest...you're talking about Elvis Presley and those guys. The Charleston was well received all over the world. Now, why didn't James P. have thirty-five million dollars to divide like the Rolling Stones on somebody else's song? What happened? How did it happen? And you gotta remember, too, that we're speaking of music and style that...many of the songs that were written by the white musicians were played and became popular with the blacks, like "Lady Be Good." A lot of people thought that Count Basie wrote "Lady Be Good." You know who wrote "Lady Be Good," right? Do you know?
Yeah, George. And you know, in other songs, in other compositions, in other...let's see, like "Ballin' the Jack." Chris...

Chris Smith wrote "Ballin' the Jack." But there was a dance called "Ballin' the Jack." And then, on and on, and I can think of a series of songs, you know what I mean, and these songs had a dance to go along with it. So I think that the dancing and the music are so interrelated that you have...when you think of one you have to think of the other. Sometimes, maybe, the dancers...I think like in the case of the Charleston,
I think that the dance was out before the song. But it's amazing, though, how related they were to each other.
